 8th Pay Commission: Performance pay, variable pay and bonus; what's on the table now
 Personal Finance News
 8th Pay Commission: Performance pay, variable pay and bonus; what's on the table now
 By Upstox News Desk 4 min read | Updated on November 09, 2026, 18:50 IST
 Preferred news source Select Upstox as your Preferred news source SUMMARY
 The question before the 8th Pay Commission is whether the performance pay or variable pay will be funded in addition to the bonus and PLB employees already receive, or carved out of them. 
 7th CPC said performance pay depends on APARs and RFD ratings, which depend on reporting officers. | Representational image/AI generated
 The 6th Central Pay Commission (CPC) had proposed a Performance Related Incentive Scheme (PRIS) run through Results Framework Documents (RFD), with awards required to be revenue neutral and had to be funded out of savings generated by the individual departments. However, it failed on four counts, according to the 7th Pay Commission report:

 First, the scheme was voluntary. It was not binding on the departments.
 Second, the scheme was dependent on savings generated by the department.
 Third, without a credible performance measurement methodology, the scheme was difficult to operationalise.
 Fourth, the RFD which had just been introduced in the Central Government was yet to take roots.
 The 7th CPC recommended performance related pay for every category of central government employees. It also recommended that such a pay should absorb the existing bonus schemes.
 The 7th CPC report noted that "there should not be automatic payment of bonus and all existing schemes of payment of bonuses should be linked to productivity". In Chapter 15, the 7th CPC report carried the operative recommendation, saying, "the Commission recommends introduction of the Performance Related Pay for all categories of Central Government employees, based on quality RFDs, reformed APARs and broad Guidelines".
 It further said, "The Commission also recommends that the PRP should subsume the existing Bonus schemes," and where departments lagged, the existing bonus schemes "should be reviewed and linked with increased profitability/productivity under well-defined financial parameters".
 Against the above history, the memorandums of staff bodies before the 8th Central Pay Commission (CPC) have asked for performance pay as an addition to salary revision, not as a replacement. 
 The Ministerial Staff Association (MSA) noted that clerical work has moved to "complex digital platforms such as PFMS, GeM, and eOffice" yet "there is no performance-related pay (PRP) to reward efficiency and accuracy in these digital workflows." It has proposed a Digital Efficiency Incentive plus a system where top performers "receive a percentage of their basic pay as 'Variable Pay' based on annual performance appraisals (APARs)".
 The Indian Railways Technical Supervisors' Association (IRTSA) has sought group incentives, asking that "a Group Incentive Scheme be introduced in all the Coaching & Wagon Depots & Sick Lines on the Railways" extended to technical departments.
 The Federation of National Postal Organisations (FNPO) has proposed an "Excellence Premium: An additional 5–10% bonus for Post Offices or units that exceed annual revenue targets".
 Every union demand is additive, in other words extra money for extra output, alongside a bonus fixed by days and a statutory floor. In contrast, the 7th CPC's framework was substitutive: one scheme replacing another.
 If the 8th CPC adopts the 7th CPC's logic, employees may have to forgo a guaranteed benefit in exchange for a contingent one. In view of this, the Railway Senior Citizens Welfare Society (RSCWS) has proposed safeguards that would be needed. It said incentives "should remain supplementary and should not replace or weaken the established pay structure such as basic pay, increments, and allowances."
 The RSCWS further said they should not be used as a substitute for regular pay revisions or as a means to control long-term financial liabilities, with pension staying "linked with stable components of pay rather than variable incentives." And on bonus, it said, "Bonus payments should remain simple, predictable and not overly dependent on complex performance metrics".
 However, a practical objection follows from the 7th CPC's own report. It noted that performance pay depends on APARs and RFD ratings, which depend on reporting officers, moderation committees and departmental targets. In contrast, a bonus calculated at 78 days' wages, or at the statutory 8.33% floor, does not. Hence, for a category where output cannot be cleanly measured, a move from the second to the first could transfer risk rather than rewarding performance.
 The question before the 8th CPC is therefore narrower than it looks. It is not whether performance pay should exist; as even the 7th CPC said it should, and the unions are not opposing it. It is whether it will be funded in addition to the bonus and PLB employees already receive, or carved out of them.
